channel.title: The Librarian's Notebook
channel.description: A commonplace book kept by Mr. Librarian: notes on science and technology, on the world and its news, on the arts, and on whatever else didn't belong in the Ledger, the Regimen or the road. Explainers over hot takes; the working shown; one reader's opinions, labelled as such.

item.title: GLP-1 Drugs: What the Evidence Shows, Organ by Organ
item.description: A standing page on the benefits being claimed for GLP-1 drugs beyond weight loss, sorted by how strong the evidence is: four large randomized trials, one mechanism study, two observational signals, and a new preprint that says semaglutide turned back the proteomic age of the heart by 2 to 4 years.

item.title: The Minimum Wage: What It Was For, What It Buys Now, and Whether a Fast-Food Job Should Pay a Living
item.description: A standing page on the US minimum wage, refreshed as the numbers move. The 1938 law's 25 cents is about $5.92 in today's money, yet it was roughly 40% of the average factory wage while $7.25 is about 19% of average pay now. As of October 7, 2026, California's fast-food floor is $20 and its general floor rises to $17.40 on January 1.

item.title: The Houthis Took the Bab al-Mandab Strait: What It Means for Oil, and What the US Is Likely to Do
item.description: In September the Houthis took the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab strait, including Perim (Mayyun) Island, just as Iran's closure of Hormuz had pushed Saudi oil onto the Red Sea. Here is why that narrow gap matters, how much oil moves through it, and why Washington has so far declined to strike.

item.title: The Global Oil Crisis: Where Things Stand
item.description: A standing page on the oil war, rewritten as it moves. As of October 6: Gulf crude exports are back around pre-war levels, but by pipeline and by shuttle tanker under daily attack, not through an open strait; Brent is near $100, 38% above where it started; the Red Sea exit is contested; and the Black Sea has become a second front.

item.title: Siberia Plague Death: What We Know, What's Disputed, What Would Change the Picture
item.description: A standing page on the death of an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute lab worker, rewritten as the story moves. As of October 7: roughly 200 contacts, about 60% tested, none positive for plague, and an unconfirmed Daily Mail report of a second death; Russian officials now say "pneumonia of unknown origin"; the cause, the date of death and the way she was exposed are all still disputed.

item.title: Your Voicemail Can Hand Over Your Telegram Login Code — How to Lock It Down on iPhone
item.description: A post on X describes an account takeover that never touched the victim's phone: a jammed line sent Telegram's "code by phone call" to voicemail, and the attacker listened in. What happened, why it works, and the iPhone settings that close it.

item.title: Amazon's Antitrust Trial Has 17 States — and Not the One It's In
item.description: The FTC's monopoly case against Amazon is heard in Seattle, but Washington's attorney general isn't one of the 17 states that sued alongside the agency. The October 13 trial date in this week's headlines is also out of date — the bench trial is now set for March 29, 2027.

item.title: The Institute Built to Prevent This Had the Accident
item.description: A 28-year-old lab worker at Russia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute died October 1 of suspected pneumonic plague, and nearly 200 people who had contact with her are now under medical observation. Officials haven't settled on how she was exposed — a broken test tube in the lab, or a recent trip near an active natural outbreak on the Mongolian border — and that gap matters more than the headline.

item.title: Track Four: "Feel the AGI"
item.description: A four-and-a-half-minute music video dressed up as the sleeve and run-out groove of a vinyl record plays "Feel the AGI" as a country-gospel revival number, setting the AI-safety community's own private vocabulary — Moloch, the orthogonality thesis, p(doom), the fire alarm, the context window — as the verses of a tent-meeting hymn. Fourth entry in the Notebook's running AI-music collection.

item.title: The Supermarket Pub Beat Lidl to Pennsylvania by Seventeen Years
item.description: Lidl just opened what it's calling the world's first supermarket pub, in Northern Ireland — a clever workaround for a liquor-licensing dead end. A Pennsylvania grocery chain built the same thing in 2009, and the reason it never became the industry norm has nothing to do with imagination and everything to do with fifty different states writing fifty different alcohol laws.

item.title: Track Three: "So You Think AI Is a Normal Technology"
item.description: A five-minute music video credited to Claude Opus 5.5 takes on "AI as Normal Technology," the 2025 essay arguing AI will spread at the slow pace of electricity, and calls out the essay's skeptic allies by name: Acemoglu, Solow, Baumol, Gary Marcus, Yann LeCun. It's a diss track aimed at an economics seminar. Third entry in the Notebook's running AI-music collection.

item.title: Track Two: "You're Just Running Late Tonight"
item.description: Kling AI 4.0 shipped on September 28 with a launch-day demo built to look like anything but an ad — a black-and-white concert film of a woman singing to an empty seat, one caption line letting the song's actual subject slip through. Second entry in the Notebook's running AI-music collection.

item.title: A Subduction Zone Caught in the Act of Dying
item.description: A Science Advances study led by Brandon Shuck of Louisiana State University images a tear opening in the Cascadia subduction zone's Nootka Fault Zone off northern Vancouver Island, where the subducting slab has already dropped about 5 kilometres — evidence, the authors argue, that subduction zones can shut down piece by piece rather than all at once.

item.title: Track One: The Song Claude Wrote and Has Never Heard
item.description: An X user gave Claude Opus 5.5 free rein and asked it to introduce itself. It wrote a full song about who it thinks it is — lyrics, chords, and a music video coded frame by frame — then said, in its own caption, that it had never heard the result. That turns out to be a literally true, checkable claim about how the pipeline was built, not a philosophical one. First entry in a running collection of AI-made music worth a look.

item.title: Two Sea Spiders Nobody Had Named in Nearly a Hundred Years
item.description: A University of British Columbia master's thesis turns up two sea spider species new to science in the Salish Sea — the first described there in almost a century — including a red-eyed, three-lipped species named for the hairy spines on its legs, found on scientific dives to 18 metres and confirmed with DNA barcoding.

item.title: It Took Its Inventor a Month. The Record Is Now 2.76 Seconds.
item.description: Ernő Rubik built the first Rubik's Cube in 1974 to work out a problem in how solid objects can move, and then needed about a month to solve it himself. The official record now belongs to a nine-year-old in Poland at 2.76 seconds. Here is how a Hungarian classroom model became a 1980s craze, and why the times fell so far once the kids came back to it.

item.title: A Comet Carrying Someone Else's Recipe for Water
item.description: A paper led by Kenji Furuya of Japan's RIKEN institute finds that the water boiling off our solar system's third interstellar visitor, 3I/ATLAS, carries a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio tens of times higher than any comet native to our own solar system — a chemical fingerprint the authors say points to a colder, more metal-poor stellar nursery than the one that built the Sun.
